savant

sa-VAHNT -- from French savant, 'knowing,' rooted in Latin sapere, 'to know, be wise.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Savant is a person of profound, specialized learning or knowledge in a particular field.

Even the ship's veteran navigators deferred to the young apprentice, a genuine savant when it came to reading storm patterns in the clouds.

Example

The young savant could name every country's capital and flag by age seven, though he still needed help tying his shoes.

The child's extraordinary, specialized knowledge -- far beyond his years -- is exactly what makes him a savant.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scholar: A scholar builds knowledge through formal study — lectures, research degrees, years inside a university. A savant's learning can come from anywhere; what marks a savant is how strikingly deep the knowledge itself runs, not the training behind it.

prodigy: A prodigy is a young person whose remarkable ability appears unusually early — mastering the violin at ten. A savant can be any age; the word points at the astonishing depth of the learning, not the age of the learner.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

novice: a person new to and inexperienced in a field

dilettante: a person with only a superficial interest or knowledge in something

Where it sits · how deep the learning runs — expert → savant → sage

expert vs. savant: Expert is weaker than savant: an expert knows her field thoroughly and can answer most questions in it, but a savant's learning runs far deeper — a profound command that even the experts seek out.

sage vs. savant: Sage is stronger than savant on this scale: a savant commands profound knowledge of one field, but the village sage people cross three counties to consult has gone further — learning ripened into life-guiding wisdom.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — savant (< French savoir)

root — savant (< French savoir): knowing, to know (French, from Latin sapere)

Put it together

Put it together: Savant comes directly from the French word for 'knowing,' itself from Latin sapere, 'to know or be wise' -- English simply borrowed the whole word rather than building it from reusable English pieces.

Use the root in a new word: savoir-faire

Use the root in a new word: savoir-faire: Savoir-faire, literally 'knowing how to do,' is a related French borrowing meaning the ability to act appropriately in any situation.

Word Choice

Savant usually implies a strikingly deep, sometimes narrow expertise -- someone people specifically seek out for their specialized knowledge, rather than just anyone who is generally smart.
